opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the biggest thing was just closing the gap between the narrative and the reality. From the outside, especially in the U.S., there's a tendency to treat "Chinese AI" as one monolithic thing, either a looming threat or a bunch of fast followers copying what we do. When you're actually in the room with researchers, that framing falls apart pretty quickly. These are people who care about the same technical problems we do: how to make post-training work better, how to get reasoning to scale, how to build good evaluations, how to release open models that people actually use. The conversations felt very familiar.

The second thing was getting a sense of the culture and the constraints they work under. You read papers and look at model releases, but you don't really understand the tradeoffs a team is making until you hear how they think about compute, talent, and what they choose to prioritize. A lot of the efficiency-focused work that comes out of these labs makes a lot more sense once you understand the environment it's coming from. It's not just clever engineering for its own sake. It's a response to real limits, and that pushes people toward creative solutions.

And third, it reinforced for me why open models matter so much. Many of these labs are deeply committed to releasing weights, and they see openness as both a research strategy and a way to build influence and trust globally. As someone who works on open models in the U.S., that was a bit of a wake-up call. If we care about the open ecosystem being shaped by American values and institutions, we can't just assume that will happen by default. We have to actually invest in it.

So more than any single technical insight, the value was in the human context: understanding who these people are, what motivates them, and how much of the future of open AI is being built over there right now.

r001.rationale: The response says the visit provided human context by hearing researchers explain how they think and understanding what motivates them, presenting this as a key value of the visit.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the most valuable thing was how much it corrected my priors. From the outside, when you're sitting in the US reading papers and release notes from DeepSeek or Qwen or Moonshot, you build up this model of what those labs are like, and a lot of it is just projection. You assume they're structured like a US lab, that the incentives are the same, that the people think about the field the same way. And a lot of that is wrong in subtle ways.

The first thing that stood out was how young the teams are. The median age at a lot of these places is noticeably lower than what you'd see at a frontier lab in the US. These are people who finished their PhDs or even just undergrad in the last few years, and they're being handed real responsibility over training runs. There's an energy there that reminded me of what OpenAI felt like around 2019 or 2020, before it got big and institutional.

The second thing is that they're paying attention to everything. Every blog post, every paper, every tweet from Western researchers, they've read it, often more carefully than people here have. The information asymmetry runs almost entirely in one direction. They know what we're doing. We mostly don't know what they're doing, partly because of language, partly because a lot of the discourse happens on WeChat and Zhihu and places that just don't get translated.

And then the third thing, which I think gets underrated, is that the open weight strategy is not a gimmick to them. When I'd ask why they release models openly, the answers were pretty consistent. It's about talent attraction, it's about building an ecosystem, and there's a genuine belief that in the absence of being able to buy the most compute, you win on distribution and adoption. That's a coherent strategy. It's not just "we're releasing because we can't compete at the top," which is the lazy read you hear a lot.

I came back thinking that the gap, to the extent there is one, is mostly a compute and infrastructure gap, not a talent or ideas gap. And that's a very different thing to plan around.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes learning why labs release models openly, but frames the central value of visiting as correcting prior assumptions. It does not identify hearing builders explain their motivations in their own words as a central value.

astra-6.text: The most valuable part was getting a feel for how people think about the work. From the outside, you see model releases and benchmark scores, but those don’t tell you much about a team’s priorities or the questions they’re wrestling with. In person, you can have that back-and-forth: What do you think matters next? What’s holding you back? What are you excited about? It helps you build a more nuanced picture than treating Chinese AI labs as one monolithic thing.

In person, you can ask follow-up questions: What are you excited about? What’s hard? How do you decide what to work on next? Those conversations give you a much richer picture than a leaderboard does. And they help you recognize where you’re making assumptions rather than actually understanding what a team is trying to do.
